title: Operating a Vector Database
description: Sharding, replication, backups, quality monitoring, and cost control once a vector database is in production.

lessons.title: Sharding and Replication
lessons.description: How a vector index stops being 'one machine's problem' as your data grows.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain the difference between sharding and replication and why a vector database needs both at scale.

sections.title: ✂️ Sharding: splitting the data
sections.content: Sharding splits your vectors across multiple machines, each holding a subset. A query typically fans out to every shard, collects candidate results from each, and merges them — the same 'scatter-gather' pattern used in distributed search engines generally. Sharding is what lets you scale storage and query throughput past what a single machine's RAM and CPU can handle.

sections.title: 🪞 Replication: copying the data
sections.content: Replication keeps multiple copies of the same shard on different machines, so a machine failure doesn't lose data or take search offline. Replicas also let you spread read traffic across more machines, increasing throughput even without adding new data.

sections.title: ⚖️ Consistency trade-offs
sections.content: When a vector is updated or deleted, replicas may briefly disagree until the change propagates — the same eventual-consistency trade-off you'd meet in any distributed data store. For most search use cases, a few seconds of staleness for a newly-added document is an acceptable trade against availability and throughput; for a compliance-driven deletion, it usually is not, and needs explicit handling.

sections.title: 🔗 Where this connects
sections.content: This is the same operational thinking the MLOps and Cloud courses apply to model-serving infrastructure — redundancy against failure, and horizontal scaling against load — just applied to the vector index instead of the model itself.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
A tiny hash-based shard assignment function, plus a toy function for routing a read to one of a shard's replicas:

```python
import hashlib

# A tiny, illustrative sharding + replica-routing scheme (NOT production code).

NUM_SHARDS = 4
REPLICAS_PER_SHARD = 3


def shard_for(vector_id, num_shards=NUM_SHARDS):
    # A stable hash of the id decides which shard owns this vector.
    digest = hashlib.sha256(vector_id.encode()).hexdigest()
    return int(digest, 16) % num_shards


def replicas_for(shard_id, replicas_per_shard=REPLICAS_PER_SHARD):
    # Each shard has a fixed set of replica node names.
    return [f"shard{shard_id}-replica{r}" for r in range(replicas_per_shard)]


def route_read(vector_id, replica_health, num_shards=NUM_SHARDS):
    # Route a read to the first *healthy* replica of the owning shard.
    shard_id = shard_for(vector_id, num_shards)
    for replica in replicas_for(shard_id):
        if replica_health.get(replica, True):
            return replica
    raise RuntimeError(f"No healthy replica available for shard {shard_id}")


ids = ["doc-1", "doc-2", "doc-3", "doc-4", "doc-5"]
placement = {vid: shard_for(vid) for vid in ids}

replica_health = {"shard3-replica0": False, "shard3-replica1": False}

print(placement)                                  # which shard owns each id
print(route_read("doc-2", replica_health))        # skips down replicas, picks a healthy one
```

`shard_for` always sends a given `vector_id` to the same shard, since a stable hash produces the same digest every time — this is what lets every node compute placement independently without a lookup table. `route_read` shows the replication side: it walks `replicas_for(shard_id)` in order and returns the first replica that `replica_health` doesn't mark as down, which is exactly how replicas let reads keep working through a node failure.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Choosing a non-uniform or poorly distributed hash for shard assignment.** A hash that clusters many ids onto the same shard creates a 'hot shard' that takes disproportionate load while others sit idle, defeating the point of sharding.

**Treating replica reads as always perfectly fresh.** Because replication is typically eventually consistent, routing a read to a replica right after a write can return stale data; code that assumes every replica is instantly up to date will occasionally serve wrong answers.

**Resharding by simply changing the shard count without a migration plan.** Changing `num_shards` changes which shard almost every id hashes to, so vectors need to be physically moved to their new shard — flipping the number without migrating the data silently breaks lookups.

questions.question: Sharding a vector database primarily helps you scale
options: Storage capacity and query throughput beyond what one machine can handle
The accuracy of the embedding model
The number of distance metrics available
The size of a single vector's dimensionality
questions.explanation: Sharding distributes data and load across machines, which is what lets the system grow past single-machine limits.

questions.question: What does replication protect against?
options: Data loss and search downtime if a machine fails
Slow embedding model inference
Poor recall from an under-tuned index
Cross-tenant data leakage
questions.explanation: Replication keeps redundant copies of data so a hardware or node failure doesn't take the index offline or lose data.

questions.question: Why might eventual consistency between replicas be acceptable for a newly-added search document but not for a compliance-driven deletion?
options: Because a few seconds of staleness costs little for a new addition, but a deletion for compliance reasons may need to be guaranteed complete
Because replicas can never be inconsistent for any reason
Because deletions are always instant across all replicas by default
Because additions are always slower than deletions
questions.explanation: The acceptable staleness window depends on the consequence of being wrong — compliance deletions typically need stronger guarantees than routine additions.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what pattern does a sharded query typically follow?
options: It fans out to every shard, collects candidates from each, and merges the results — the 'scatter-gather' pattern
It queries a single randomly chosen shard and ignores the rest
It queries only the shard with the least data
It requires the client to know which shard holds the answer in advance
questions.explanation: The lesson describes sharded search as scatter-gather: fan out to every shard, then merge each shard's candidates.

questions.question: According to the lesson, besides protecting against data loss, what other benefit does replication provide?
options: It spreads read traffic across more machines, increasing throughput even without adding new data
It automatically re-embeds the corpus with a newer model
It eliminates the need for sharding entirely
It reduces the dimensionality of stored vectors
questions.explanation: The lesson notes replicas let you spread read traffic across more machines, increasing throughput even without adding new data.

questions.question: In the code example, why does shard_for(vector_id) return the same shard id every time it's called with the same vector_id?
options: Because it hashes the id with a stable hash function (sha256) and takes the digest modulo num_shards, which is deterministic
Because it looks the id up in a cache that never changes
Because vector_id is always converted to shard 0
Because Python dictionaries preserve insertion order
questions.explanation: shard_for computes hashlib.sha256(vector_id.encode()).hexdigest() and reduces it mod num_shards — a deterministic hash, so the same id always maps to the same shard.

questions.question: In the route_read example, what happens when the first replica(s) for a shard are marked unhealthy in replica_health?
options: route_read skips them and returns the first replica in the list that is not marked unhealthy
route_read immediately raises an error even if a healthy replica exists
route_read routes the read to a different shard entirely
route_read ignores replica_health and always returns replica0
questions.explanation: route_read loops through replicas_for(shard_id) in order and returns the first one for which replica_health.get(replica, True) is truthy, skipping unhealthy ones.

questions.question: Per 'Common mistakes', why is changing num_shards without a migration plan a problem?
options: Because it changes which shard almost every id hashes to, so vectors must be physically moved or lookups silently break
Because num_shards cannot be changed once an index is created
Because it has no effect on hash-based shard assignment
Because it only affects newly written vectors, never existing ones
questions.explanation: Since shard assignment is hash(id) mod num_shards, changing num_shards reshuffles almost every id's target shard, requiring data migration.

lessons.title: Backups and Disaster Recovery
lessons.description: Your embeddings are expensive to regenerate. Treat losing them as a real incident, not an inconvenience.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain why vector index backups matter and what a recovery plan needs to account for.

sections.title: 💸 Regenerating embeddings isn't free
sections.content: If you lose your vector index with no backup, recovery means re-embedding your entire corpus from scratch — real compute cost and real time, and if the original documents themselves are also gone, the data may be unrecoverable entirely. This is a stronger argument for backups than most people expect from 'just a search index.'

sections.title: 📸 What to back up
sections.content: The vector index itself (or its source data plus a script to rebuild it), any metadata payloads, and — often overlooked — the exact embedding model version and preprocessing steps used to produce the vectors, since re-embedding with a different model version produces vectors that are not comparable to the old ones (a problem the next lesson covers directly).

sections.title: 🧯 Test your restore, not just your backup
sections.content: A backup you've never restored from is a hypothesis, not a safety net — the same lesson the MLOps course's rollback lesson made about model artifacts. Periodically practice a full restore in a non-production environment and time how long it takes; that number is your actual recovery time objective, not whatever number was assumed when the backup policy was written.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
A toy backup-manifest structure, plus a restore-verification function that checks a checksum before trusting a restored vector set:

```python
import hashlib
import json

# A tiny, illustrative backup manifest + restore verification (NOT production code).


def make_manifest(vectors, model_version, preprocessing_steps):
    payload = json.dumps(vectors, sort_keys=True).encode()
    checksum = hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest()
    return {
        "model_version": model_version,
        "preprocessing_steps": preprocessing_steps,
        "vector_count": len(vectors),
        "checksum": checksum,
    }


def restore_and_verify(vectors, manifest):
    payload = json.dumps(vectors, sort_keys=True).encode()
    recomputed = hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest()
    checks = {
        "checksum_matches": recomputed == manifest["checksum"],
        "count_matches": len(vectors) == manifest["vector_count"],
    }
    checks["restore_ok"] = all(checks.values())
    return checks


vectors = {"doc-1": [0.1, 0.2], "doc-2": [0.3, 0.4]}
manifest = make_manifest(vectors, model_version="embed-v3", preprocessing_steps=["lowercase", "strip_html"])

# Simulate a clean restore of the same data:
restored_ok = restore_and_verify(vectors, manifest)

# Simulate a corrupted restore (one vector silently changed):
corrupted = {"doc-1": [0.1, 0.2], "doc-2": [0.3, 0.9]}
restored_bad = restore_and_verify(corrupted, manifest)

print(manifest)
print(restored_ok)     # checksum_matches: True, restore_ok: True
print(restored_bad)    # checksum_matches: False, restore_ok: False
```

`make_manifest` records not just a checksum but the `model_version` and `preprocessing_steps` alongside it, so a future restore can tell whether the vectors it's looking at were even produced the same way. `restore_and_verify` recomputes the checksum from the restored data and only reports `restore_ok: True` when it exactly matches the manifest's original checksum — notice that a single changed value anywhere in `corrupted` is enough to flip `checksum_matches` to `False`.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Backing up vectors without the embedding model version or preprocessing steps.** A restored vector set that isn't tagged with exactly how it was produced can't be safely compared or merged with vectors added after the backup, since even a minor model version bump changes the embedding space.

**Assuming a backup is good because the backup job reported success.** A backup job can complete without error and still be silently corrupted or incomplete; only a verified restore (checksum, count, or an actual restore drill) confirms the backup is usable.

**Never timing a restore until an actual outage forces it.** Discovering during a real incident that a "quick restore" actually takes six hours turns a recoverable outage into a much longer one — the time to learn your real recovery time objective is during a practice drill, not a live incident.

questions.question: Why can losing a vector index without a backup be more costly than losing an ordinary cache?
options: Rebuilding it means re-embedding the entire corpus, which costs real compute and time, and may be impossible if source documents are also gone
Vector indexes are always automatically backed up by the cloud provider
Vector databases cannot be backed up at all
Losing a vector index has no effect on the application
questions.explanation: Unlike a simple cache, a lost vector index isn't a cheap rebuild — regenerating embeddings at scale is a real cost, and total data loss is possible if source documents are gone too.

questions.question: A complete vector database backup should include
options: The vectors/metadata plus the exact embedding model version and preprocessing steps used to produce them
Only the raw text documents, never the vectors
Only the index configuration file
Nothing beyond the vectors themselves
questions.explanation: Without knowing the exact model and preprocessing used, restored vectors may not be comparable to any vectors added later.

questions.question: Why is testing a restore at least as important as taking a backup?
options: Because an untested backup is only a hypothesis about recoverability, not a proven safety net
Because restoring is always faster than backing up
Because backups expire after one use
Because restore tests are required by vector database vendors
questions.explanation: Only a practiced restore reveals whether the backup actually works and how long recovery really takes.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what does periodically timing a full restore actually give you?
options: Your real recovery time objective, rather than whatever number was assumed when the backup policy was written
A discount on cloud storage costs
A higher embedding model accuracy
Automatic detection of filter misconfigurations
questions.explanation: The lesson says timing a practiced restore is what tells you your actual recovery time objective, not an assumed figure from the backup policy.

questions.question: The lesson compares 'test your restore' to which idea from another course?
options: The MLOps course's rollback lesson about model artifacts
The RAG course's chunking strategy lesson
The Cloud course's networking lesson
The Math course's PCA lesson
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly draws the parallel to the MLOps course's rollback lesson, which made the same point about model artifacts.

questions.question: In the code example, what information does make_manifest store alongside the checksum?
options: The model_version and preprocessing_steps used to produce the vectors, plus the vector_count
The full source text of every document
The IP address of the backup server
Nothing else — only the checksum is stored
questions.explanation: make_manifest returns a dict containing model_version, preprocessing_steps, vector_count, and checksum.

questions.question: In the corrupted-restore simulation, why does restore_and_verify(corrupted, manifest) report checksum_matches as False?
options: Because one vector's value was changed, so the recomputed sha256 hash over the corrupted data no longer matches the checksum stored in the manifest
Because the corrupted dict has a different number of keys than the original
Because restore_and_verify always returns False for any input
Because json.dumps cannot serialize the corrupted dictionary
questions.explanation: restore_and_verify recomputes a sha256 checksum from the given vectors; changing even one value in corrupted produces a different digest, so it no longer equals manifest['checksum'].

questions.question: Per 'Common mistakes', why is a backup job reporting 'success' not sufficient proof the backup is usable?
options: Because a backup job can complete without error while still being silently corrupted or incomplete; only a verified restore confirms it works
Because backup jobs never report their status
Because success reports are only valid for one hour
Because a successful backup job always means the restore will fail
questions.explanation: The mistakes section warns that job-reported success doesn't guarantee usability — only a checksum check or actual restore drill does.

lessons.title: Monitoring Vector Search Quality
lessons.description: Uptime dashboards won't tell you that search results have quietly gotten worse.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: List signals worth monitoring for a production vector search system beyond basic uptime.

sections.title: 📉 Quality can degrade silently
sections.content: A vector search system can be 'up' — responding to queries with normal latency — while returning steadily worse results, because the underlying data distribution shifted, because a filter is silently dropping too much of the index, or because an index rebuild used the wrong configuration. None of this shows up on a standard infrastructure dashboard.

sections.title: 📡 Signals worth tracking
sections.content: Query latency percentiles and error rates (standard infrastructure monitoring). Result-count anomalies — a spike in queries returning zero or very few results, which often signals an overly strict filter or an indexing gap. Sampled recall against a small labeled set, re-run periodically, the same way the RAG and LLMOps courses insisted on periodic evaluation rather than a one-time check. Downstream signals like click-through or user feedback, when available, since they reflect real relevance better than any proxy metric.

sections.title: 🚨 Alert on the business signal, not just the infrastructure signal
sections.content: 'Search latency is fine' is necessary but not sufficient — pairing infrastructure monitoring with a periodic quality check is what catches the failure mode that matters most: a system that's technically healthy but functionally useless, which is exactly the kind of silent degradation the LLMOps course's continuous-evaluation lesson also warned about for LLM outputs.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Monitoring only infrastructure metrics like latency and uptime.** A system can be fast and 'up' while quietly returning worse results, so infrastructure health alone gives false confidence about search quality.

**Using an unbounded, all-time average for a quality metric.** Averaging recall over the system's entire lifetime buries a recent regression under months of good historical data, delaying detection of exactly the kind of drift the lesson warns about.

**Treating a one-time launch benchmark as sufficient forever.** Data distributions, filters, and index configurations all change after launch; a recall number measured once at launch says nothing about quality six months later without periodic re-measurement.

questions.question: Why can a vector search system look 'healthy' on an infrastructure dashboard while actually performing poorly?
options: Because result quality can degrade silently even when latency and uptime remain normal
Because infrastructure dashboards always include a recall metric by default
Because vector databases cannot experience quality degradation
Because latency and quality are always perfectly correlated
questions.explanation: Standard uptime/latency dashboards don't capture relevance quality, which can quietly degrade for reasons infrastructure monitoring won't catch.

questions.question: A spike in queries returning zero or very few results often signals
options: An overly strict filter or an indexing gap
Perfect recall
A hardware upgrade
A successful reranking pass
questions.explanation: Sudden drops in result counts are a practical early signal that something in filtering or indexing has gone wrong.

questions.question: Why is periodic sampled recall measurement valuable in production, not just during initial benchmarking?
options: Because it catches quality degradation that infrastructure metrics like latency and uptime cannot detect on their own
Because recall never changes once an index is built
Because it replaces the need for latency monitoring entirely
Because sampled recall is required to compute storage costs
questions.explanation: Ongoing recall checks act like the continuous evaluation practices from LLMOps and RAG, surfacing quality drift that pure infra monitoring would miss.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why are downstream signals like click-through or user feedback valuable when available?
options: Because they reflect real relevance better than any proxy metric
Because they are cheaper to collect than latency metrics
Because they replace the need for a labeled evaluation set entirely
Because they are the only signal infrastructure dashboards can show
questions.explanation: The lesson lists downstream signals like click-through and feedback as valuable specifically because they reflect real relevance more directly than proxy metrics.

questions.question: What does the lesson identify as the failure mode that matters most, and that pairing infrastructure and quality monitoring is meant to catch?
options: A system that's technically healthy but functionally useless
A system that is completely offline
A system with too many replicas
A system that costs too much to run
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly names 'technically healthy but functionally useless' as the failure mode that alerting on business signals, not just infrastructure signals, is meant to catch.

questions.question: In the code example, why doesn't make_recall_monitor's record function raise an alert on the very first few samples passed to it?
options: Because the sliding window hasn't filled to window_size yet, so it returns a 'warming up' result instead of comparing to baseline
Because the baseline_recall value is set to 0 initially
Because the deque silently discards the first samples
Because RECALL_DROP_THRESHOLD only applies after 100 samples
questions.explanation: record checks `if len(window) < window_size: return {"alert": False, "reason": "warming up"}` before comparing against baseline_recall, so early calls can't yet trigger an alert.

questions.question: In check_latency_p99([12, 15, 14, 13, 900, 16, 15], threshold_ms=100), what does the function report?
options: alert: True, because the 900ms outlier lands at the 99th-percentile index of the sorted latencies, exceeding the threshold
alert: False, because the average latency is well under 100ms
alert: True, because every latency in the list exceeds 100ms
alert: False, because p99 is not computed from sorted data
questions.explanation: sorted_latencies places 900 near the top of the sorted list; with only 7 samples the p99 index lands on that outlier, so p99_ms is 900, which exceeds threshold_ms=100 and sets alert to True.

questions.question: Per 'Common mistakes', why is using an unbounded, all-time average for a quality metric a problem?
options: Because it buries a recent regression under months of good historical data, delaying detection of drift
Because all-time averages are mathematically impossible to compute
Because it makes the monitoring code run out of memory immediately
Because it only works for latency metrics, never recall
questions.explanation: The mistakes section explains that an all-time average dilutes a recent drop with historical good data, which is exactly why the code example uses a bounded sliding window instead.

lessons.title: Cost Optimization at Scale
lessons.description: Vector search bills scale with dimensions, vector count, and replication — and each has its own lever.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Name at least three concrete levers for reducing vector database cost without abandoning your quality requirements.

sections.title: 📉 Reduce what you store
sections.content: Lower-dimensional embeddings (a smaller model, or dimensionality reduction like the PCA covered in the Math course) shrink memory and compute per vector. Quantization — the PQ technique from earlier in this course, or simpler scalar quantization — shrinks stored vector size directly, often the single biggest lever at scale.

sections.title: 🗑️ Store less of it
sections.content: Not every document needs to live in the hot index forever — tiering older or rarely-queried vectors to cheaper storage, or deleting embeddings for deleted source documents (an easy thing to forget, and a slow leak on your bill), both reduce cost directly.

sections.title: ⚙️ Tune replication and infrastructure to actual need
sections.content: Over-provisioned replicas for a system that doesn't need that much redundancy or throughput is pure waste — right-size replication to your actual availability and QPS requirements, revisited periodically as traffic patterns change, rather than set once at launch and left alone.

sections.title: 💵 Measure cost per query, not just total spend
sections.content: Total infrastructure spend without a per-query or per-tenant cost breakdown makes it hard to know which lever will actually move the number — the same 'cost per unit of value' discipline the LLMOps course applied to token costs, applied here to vector search queries.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Comparing configurations by total monthly cost alone, without normalizing by query volume or vector count.** A configuration that looks cheaper in absolute terms might actually cost more per query once traffic differences are accounted for, hiding the real comparison.

**Cutting replicas to save cost without checking the availability and throughput requirement first.** Fewer replicas directly reduces both fault tolerance and read capacity — a cost win that turns into an incident if it drops below what the product actually needs.

**Forgetting to delete embeddings for documents that were deleted elsewhere in the system.** Orphaned vectors keep consuming storage (and get multiplied by every replica) indefinitely, quietly inflating the bill for data nobody can even query for anymore.

questions.question: Which of these is a direct lever for reducing vector database storage cost?
options: Quantizing vectors or using lower-dimensional embeddings
Increasing the number of replicas
Adding more metadata fields to every vector
Switching to exact brute-force search
questions.explanation: Quantization and lower dimensionality both directly shrink the memory footprint per vector, a major cost driver at scale.

questions.question: A commonly forgotten source of wasted vector database spend is
options: Leftover embeddings for source documents that were already deleted elsewhere
Using a distance metric other than Euclidean
Enabling metadata filtering
Running a recall benchmark
questions.explanation: Orphaned embeddings for deleted documents quietly consume storage with zero value — a slow, easy-to-miss cost leak.

questions.question: Why measure cost per query or per tenant instead of just total infrastructure spend?
options: Because it reveals which specific lever will actually reduce cost, the same way LLMOps tracks cost per token rather than just total spend
Because per-query cost is required by cloud providers
Because total spend cannot be measured for vector databases
Because per-tenant billing is illegal without it
questions.explanation: A granular cost breakdown turns 'the bill is high' into an actionable optimization target, mirroring the cost-per-unit discipline used elsewhere in this curriculum.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why should replication be right-sized 'periodically' rather than set once at launch?
options: Because traffic patterns change over time, and infrastructure sized for launch conditions can become over- or under-provisioned later
Because replicas automatically expire every month
Because launch-time replication settings are always illegal to keep
Because periodic resizing is required to keep the embedding model up to date
questions.explanation: The lesson says replication should be right-sized to actual availability and QPS needs and revisited periodically as traffic patterns change, not set once and left alone.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what technique from earlier in the course is called out as often the single biggest storage-cost lever?
options: Quantization (such as PQ or scalar quantization)
Adding more metadata filters
Switching to a different distance metric
Increasing the number of shards
questions.explanation: The lesson states quantization, including the PQ technique covered earlier in the course, is often the single biggest lever for reducing storage at scale.

questions.question: In the code example, why does scalar_quantized_3_replicas use a much smaller storage_bytes value than full_fp32_3_replicas for the same vector_count?
options: Because its bytes_per_vector is 384 instead of 1536, so storage_bytes (which multiplies bytes_per_vector by vector_count and replicas) scales down proportionally
Because it uses fewer replicas than full_fp32_3_replicas
Because it stores fewer vectors overall
Because monthly_queries is different between the two configs
questions.explanation: Both configs have replicas=3 and the same vector_count; the only difference feeding storage_bytes is bytes_per_vector (1536 vs 384), which directly scales the result.

questions.question: Based on the printed output of the code, what tradeoff does scalar_quantized_2_replicas illustrate compared to scalar_quantized_3_replicas?
options: Lower storage and lower cost_per_query, but one fewer replica's worth of redundancy and read throughput
Higher storage but identical cost_per_query
Identical storage and identical cost_per_query, differing only in name
Higher cost_per_query despite fewer replicas
questions.explanation: scalar_quantized_2_replicas shares the same bytes_per_vector as the 3-replica version but has fewer replicas and a lower monthly_infra_cost, so both storage_bytes and cost_per_query come out lower — at the cost of one fewer replica.

questions.question: Per 'Common mistakes', why is cutting replicas purely to save cost risky?
options: Because fewer replicas directly reduces fault tolerance and read capacity, which can turn a cost win into an incident if it falls below what the product needs
Because replicas have no relationship to availability or throughput
Because cutting replicas always increases storage cost
Because replica count cannot legally be changed after launch
questions.explanation: The mistakes section warns that reducing replicas without checking the actual availability/throughput requirement first can turn a cost saving into a reliability incident.
